description: As a BS Artificial Intelligence student serving as our team's Technical Lead, I specialize in transforming complex data into actionable machine learning pipelines using Python, TensorFlow, and Scikit-Learn.
summary:
PyroSight is a full-stack microgravity combustion intelligence dashboard built for the "Flame in Free Fall" challenge. It ingests all 133 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database and transforms them into a ranked, interactive, and queryable fire-safety tool for mission planners.

Using a custom Flammability Relevance Index, a physics-informed ML risk calculator, and a RAG-powered Q&A pipeline over real NASA documentation, PyroSight lets engineers instantly explore which experiments matter most for specific habitats — the ISS, a lunar base running 32% O₂, or a Mars habitat — and model the fire consequence of any atmospheric configuration in seconds.

It addresses the challenge by solving a real gap: 133 valuable experiments exist in NASA PSI, but no tool ranks, compares, or synthesises them for habitat-specific fire-safety decisions. PyroSight makes that knowledge accessible and honest — every synthetic data point is labelled, every Moon/Mars prediction is flagged as bounded inference, and real model metrics are displayed. Fire in space is catastrophic and irreversible. PyroSight helps ensure the science to prevent it is never buried in a database again.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?

PyroSight is a full-stack scientific decision-support dashboard that ingests all 133 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database — the most comprehensive public repository of microgravity combustion research — and transforms them into an interactive, ranked, and queryable fire-safety intelligence layer.

It works in three layers:

  1. Data Pipeline (Python/FastAPI backend): A pipeline fetches, parses, and validates all PSI combustion records into a structured Parquet dataset. It separates 34 genuine NASA flight runs from 75 physics-informed synthetic priors (clearly labelled throughout), then engineers multi-dimensional features — oxygen percentage, ambient pressure, gravity level, spread rate, and material type — to compute a Flammability Relevance Index (FRI) for every investigation.
  2. ML Model + Risk Calculator: A scikit-learn classifier and regressor, trained on the engineered dataset, power a live risk calculator. Users input oxygen %, pressure (kPa), and gravity level (microgravity / lunar / Martian / Earth) and receive an instant flammability risk score with confidence context — honestly reporting real cross-validation metrics (AUC 0.537, R² 0.311) rather than inflating results.
  3. RAG-Powered Insights (AI Q&A): A Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline chunks and indexes 8 NASA reference documents (PSI corpus, ISS researcher guides, SAFFIRE reports, ACME/FLEX documentation). Users can ask plain-English questions and receive cited, governance-labelled answers via the Gemini API.

The Next.js frontend presents all of this through 11 interactive pages: a ranked leaderboard, side-by-side investigation comparisons, a 2D heatmap of experimental coverage gaps, an Earth spinoffs explorer, and more.

What benefits does it have?

  • Saves mission planners hundreds of hours of manual literature review — all 133 investigations are pre-ranked, searchable, and comparable in one place.
  • Surfaces coverage gaps no one has visualised before: the Gaps & Sweep heatmap shows exactly which oxygen %, pressure, and gravity combinations have zero real experimental data, directly guiding where future NASA experiments should focus.
  • Honest by design: every synthetic data point is labelled, every Moon/Mars prediction is flagged as "bounded inference, not measured," and real (not cherry-picked) ML metrics are displayed. This makes it trustworthy for actual engineering use.
  • No backend required to run: the frontend works entirely in mock mode off real NASA PSI JSON data, meaning anyone — a researcher, a student, a mission planner — can run it instantly with just npm install && npm run dev.
  • Bridges the communication gap between raw scientific data and decision-makers who need clear, actionable fire-risk answers for specific habitat scenarios.

What is the intended impact?

The core intended impact is making microgravity fire safety data accessible and actionable for crewed deep-space mission planning.

As NASA prepares for sustained lunar presence (Artemis Moon Base, 32% O₂ at 70.3 kPa — a >50% relative oxygen increase over Earth air) and eventual Mars habitats, fire risk is one of the least-understood life-safety challenges. A fire in space cannot be treated the way a fire on Earth can — there is no quick evacuation, suppression options are limited, and flame behaviour is completely counterintuitive in microgravity.

PyroSight's intended impact is threefold:

  1. Prioritise future experiments — the coverage gap visualisation tells NASA exactly where the data holes are.
  2. Inform habitat design decisions — the risk calculator lets engineers instantly model the fire consequence of a specific atmospheric configuration before committing to it.
  3. Democratise access — an open-source, web-deployable tool means this knowledge is not locked inside a database API that requires specialist access to query.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages:

  • TypeScript / TSX (frontend)
  • Python 3.11 (backend, data pipeline, ML)

Frontend:

  • Next.js 14 (App Router) + React 18
  • Tailwind CSS 3.4
  • TanStack Query v5 (data fetching)
  • Zod v3 (schema validation)
  • Recharts v2 + custom SVG Heatmap component (visualisations)
  • Vitest v2, React Testing Library, MSW v2, Playwright (testing)

Backend / Data:

  • FastAPI + Uvicorn (REST API)
  • Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow / Parquet (data processing)
  • scikit-learn (flammability risk ML model)
  • Docker (containerisation)

AI / RAG:

  • Gemini API (LLM for RAG Q&A)
  • Custom chunker + retriever pipeline

Data Source:

  • NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database — real flight data

Version Control / Deployment:

  • Git + GitHub (github.com/fatima08-ai/PyroSight)

Hardware: Standard laptops — no specialised hardware required.

How is your project creative?

Several aspects set PyroSight apart:

  1. The Flammability Relevance Index is original. No existing tool ranks PSI investigations by multi-factor fire relevance for specific habitats. We designed the FRI from scratch combining combustion physics (spread rate, oxygen sensitivity, pressure dependence) with habitat context (gravity level, atmospheric composition) to create a single, comparable score.
  2. The coverage gap heatmap is a novel visualisation. Plotting the entire 2D oxygen/pressure/gravity parameter space and marking which cells have real data vs. zero data vs. only synthetic priors has never been done for the PSI database before. It makes invisible knowledge gaps instantly visible.
  3. Governance-first design. Most hackathon projects maximise impressive-looking outputs. We did the opposite: we explicitly show weak model metrics, label every synthetic data point, and display warnings whenever predictions leave the range of real data. This is creative precisely because it resists the temptation to overstate — and makes the tool credible for real engineering use.
  4. Dual-mode architecture. The frontend runs fully on client-side mock data sourced from real NASA PSI records, with a one-click toggle to connect to the live backend. This was a creative engineering choice that makes the project instantly runnable and demonstrable without any server infrastructure.
  5. The RAG Q&A. Letting a mission planner type "How does flame spread rate change at Martian oxygen levels?" and receive a cited, governance-labelled answer drawn from actual NASA documentation — not a hallucination — required careful RAG design with citation tracking and boundary labelling.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific honesty above all: We never conflated the synthetic physics priors with real flight data. Every design decision — labels, warnings, metric reporting — was made with the question "could this mislead an actual engineer?" in mind.
  • Data scarcity: Microgravity combustion data is genuinely rare. We accounted for this by making data provenance (real vs. synthetic) a first-class UI concept, not a footnote.
  • Habitat specificity: Different habitats (ISS, Moon Base, Mars) have fundamentally different atmospheric profiles. We built habitat-aware filtering and scoring rather than a one-size-fits-all risk number.
  • Usability without deployment: A tool only a backend engineer can run is not useful in a hackathon context. We designed the mock-data mode so judges, reviewers, and the public can run the full dashboard with a single command.
  • Scope honesty: We explicitly state that our risk scores are decision-support metrics, not NASA-STD-6001 flight certifications. We considered the ethical responsibility of building something that could influence real safety decisions.
